newsitem.title: USA: Judge refuses to order papers to take back strikers.
newsitem.headline: Judge refuses to order papers to take back strikers.

text.p: A federal judge Thursday refused to order Detroit's two newspapers to immediately take back strikers who walked off the job more than two years ago.

The National Labor Relations Board had asked U.S. District Court Judge John Corbett O'Meara for a preliminary injunction that would force the Detroit Free Press and Detroit News to put more than 1,000 strikers back to work.
About 2,500 distribution, editorial and production workers represented by six unions walked off the job on July 13, 1995, when contract talks collapsed.

In June, an administrative law judge agreed with the strikers that the papers and their joint operating agency had committed unfair labor practices. He also ordered the papers to reinstate all unfair labor practice strikers, even if it means displacing workers hired since the strike.

When the papers appealed the decision, the NLRB asked for a federal court order. The NLRB argued that by the time the lengthy appeals process is over, strikers would be gone and the collective bargaining process would be harmed.

But the papers said the judge should not interfere with the legal process. In his ruling, O'Meara said it would be premature to grant the injunction while the unfair labor practice issues work their way through the legal system, said Susie Ellwood, a spokeswoman for Detroit Newspapers Inc., which operates the two papers.
The NLRB said it was reviewing the judge's opinion would decide soon whether to appeal the decision.

"We regret that the district court did not agree that an injunction is warranted in this case. We continue to believe that we have a strong case for injunctive relief," said NLRB General Counsel Fred Feinstein in a statement.
The NLRB has 60 days to appeal the decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.
Nancy Dunn, a spokeswoman for the six unions, declined to comment on the decision until their lawyers review legal options. A news conference is planned for Friday.
The Free Press is owned by Knight-Ridder Co.. Gannett Co Inc. owns the News. The papers are editorially independent but jointly published through Detroit Newspapers.
